name: Sicilian Dragon, Levenfish Variation
summary: The Levenfish Attack (B71) meets the Dragon with an early 6.f4, aiming for e5 to hit the f6-knight before Black completes the ...g6 fianchetto.
intro: The Levenfish Variation is an early, aggressive sideline against the Sicilian Dragon, reached after 1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5.Nc3 g6 6.f4. Instead of the main-line Yugoslav Attack with Be3 and Qd2, White immediately prepares the central thrust e5, hoping to strike at the f6-knight before Black completes the kingside fianchetto with ...Bg7. The point is timing: if Black continues carelessly, the e5-break can win material or seize a lasting initiative. The Levenfish is sharper and more forcing than the strategic main lines, but it is also less critical, and with accurate play Black equalizes comfortably. It remains a useful surprise weapon for club and tournament players alike.
line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 g6 f4

sections.heading: Strategic ideas
paragraphs: The whole idea of 6.f4 is the e5-break. With the f-pawn supporting the advance, White threatens e5 to dislodge the f6-knight and open lines while Black's king is still in the centre. This gives the variation a forcing, tactical flavour quite different from the slow manoeuvring of the Yugoslav Attack. Black cannot simply play on autopilot: the routine 6...Bg7?! runs into 7.e5!, when the complications favour White. Instead Black must meet the threat head-on before continuing normal Dragon development.

Once the early e5-break is defused, play tends to settle into familiar Sicilian channels, though White's committal f4 can leave weaknesses in his camp, particularly along the a7-g1 diagonal and around the e-file. Black aims to complete the fianchetto, castle, and generate the usual Dragon counterplay against White's centre and queenside, often with the long diagonal and the open lines as key battlegrounds.

sections.heading: Main variations
paragraphs: The accurate reply is 6...Nc6!, developing while adding a defender and discouraging e5. After 7.Nxc6 bxc6 8.e5 Nd7 9.exd6 exd6 the position is roughly balanced, and 7.Be3 or 7.Nf3 lead to normal play. By contrast, the natural-looking 6...Bg7?! is a known inaccuracy because of 7.e5!, when 7...dxe5 8.fxe5 gives White a dangerous initiative, with ideas like Bb5+ exploiting Black's uncastled king.

White can also handle the position more quietly, meeting 6...Nc6 with 7.Be3 or 7.Nf3 and keeping the f4-pawn as a springboard for a later e5 or f5 advance. But the entire justification of the Levenfish is the immediate central clash, so games most often revolve around whether Black can neutralize e5. Because 6...Nc6 does so reliably, the variation is regarded as a respectable surprise weapon rather than a truly critical test of the Dragon.

sections.heading: History and background
paragraphs: The variation is named after Grigory Levenfish, a leading Soviet grandmaster of the 1920s and 1930s and a two-time Soviet champion who famously drew a match with Mikhail Botvinnik. His idea of meeting the Dragon with an early f4 and e5 predates the systematic development of the Yugoslav Attack, offering White a quick, forcing alternative to the slower main lines. Though modern theory holds that Black equalizes with precise play, the Levenfish endures as a practical try, prized for its ability to catch an unprepared Dragon player before the familiar strategic battle even begins.
